==Problem==
Mr. Harman needs to know the combined weight in pounds of three boxes he wants to mail. However, the only available scale is not accurate for weights less than <math>100</math> pounds or more than <math>150</math> pounds. So the boxes are weighed in pairs in every possible way. The results are <math>122</math>, <math>125</math> and <math>127</math> pounds. What is the combined weight in pounds of the three boxes?

<math>\textbf{(A)}\ 160\qquad
\textbf{(B)}\ 170\qquad
\textbf{(C)}\ 187\qquad
\textbf{(D)}\ 195\qquad
\textbf{(E)}\ 354</math>


==Solution 1==
Each box is weighed twice during this, so the combined weight of the three boxes is half the weight of these separate measures:

<cmath>\frac{122+125+127}{2} = \frac{374}{2} = \boxed{\textbf{(C)}\ 187}.</cmath>

==Solution 2==
Using variables <imath>a</imath>, <imath>b</imath>, and <imath>c</imath> to denote the boxes, with <imath>a \le b \le c</imath>. It is obvious that <imath>a+b=122</imath> and <imath>a+c=125</imath>, since these are the two smallest pairs. Subtracting the former equation from the latter results in <imath>c-b=3</imath>. Additionally, <imath>c+b=127</imath>. Solving for <imath>c</imath> and <imath>b</imath> gives <imath>c=65</imath> and <imath>b=62</imath>, so we can thus find <imath>a=60</imath>. Solving <imath>60+62+65=\boxed{\textbf{(C) }\ 187}</imath>

~megaboy6679

==Solution 3==

We use variables <imath>x</imath>, <imath>y</imath>, and <imath>z</imath> to denote the three boxes. We know that <imath>x+y=122</imath>, <imath>x+z=125</imath>, and <imath>y+z=127</imath>. Note that the order of the variables or equations doesn't matter as long as they are consistent. By adding all three equations, we obtain <imath>2x+2y+2z=122+125+127=374</imath>. Dividing be 2, we obtain the sum <imath>x+y+z</imath> is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) }\ 187}</imath>.

~Lightning_Fox
